top3.why: PhilaMOCA's Psychotronic Film Society hits its regular first/third-Monday slot with a night of deliberately deranged programming — the kind of gonzo, grindhouse-adjacent bill you won't find at a multiplex. It's $5 at the door, no advance ticket needed, in the tiny mausoleum-turned-microcinema on N. 12th St. The exact film is kept loose by design (the venue just warns of 'extreme subject matter') — part of the appeal is not knowing until you're in the seat.

A standing first-and-third-Monday hangout for trans and non-binary people (plus partners and allies) at Iffy Books, the anarchist bookstore that's become one of the city's steadiest queer-community anchors. No RSVP, no cover — just snacks, coffee, and a room built explicitly to be safe. Small and recurring, but exactly the kind of low-visibility community infrastructure that's easy to overlook and worth knowing about.

A DIY garage-rock/shoegaze bill at Cousin Danny's, the scrappy West Philly lounge that punches above its size for touring indie acts. Fraternal Twin and Ditch are passing through on a broader tour (they'd just played Pittsburgh), backed by locals Lo Fives and Wax Girl — a genuinely easy-to-miss weeknight show off the big-venue circuit.

top3.why: Cursive frontman Tim Kasher's directorial feature gets a rare theatrical stop at PhilaMOCA — an advance screening of his psychological horror-thriller 'Who's Watching,' about a metalhead's obsessive fixation on a coworker, ahead of its wider September release. Kasher sticks around after for a Q&A and a short acoustic set, which is the real reason to go: a one-night convergence of horror-film-nerd and indie-rock-fan Philly, not something you can catch next month. $17 at the tiny mausoleum-turned-microcinema on N. 12th St.

Vancouver's Black Pontiac bring their self-described 'DIY or die' melodic garage-rock and indie-pop to Ortlieb's, with Sunderstar and Philly's own Noshows opening. A real touring bill at a real Northern Liberties room, not a hometown filler night. $20.55, 21+, doors at 8.

A free, in-person discussion of 'Rustin's Challenge' — the book reframing Bayard Rustin, the organizer who actually built the March on Washington, around his 'Freedom Budget for All Americans' — led with Paul Prescod at the Ethical Society. Political education in the same lineage as Wooden Shoe's ed line: history read for what it can teach an organizing movement right now, not trivia about a famous speech.

top3.why: Dave Zirin's new biography of Howard Zinn gets a stop at Wooden Shoe, the city's anarchist bookstore and the natural home for it — 'The People's Historian' traces how the author of 'A People's History of the United States' became one of the 20th century's defining radical intellectuals. Exactly the kind of political-education programming Wooden Shoe's ed line exists for: history read as a toolkit, not nostalgia.

Philly DSA canvasses West Philly for Chris Rabb, the democratic-socialist candidate running for PA-03 on universal healthcare, childcare, and abolishing ICE. No experience required — new canvassers get trained and paired with a partner, then the group debriefs together after. Direct electoral organizing, and a chance to talk to actual neighbors about actual policy.

Kieślowski's Dekalog — ten hour-long films loosely built around the Ten Commandments, among the towering achievements of world cinema — gets a rare theatrical run at the Film Society Center, screened two parts a night across a special series (tonight: 3 & 4, in a 4K restoration). Not a streaming-queue watch: genuinely different on a big screen, and not a presentation you'll see return soon.

top3.why: Charles Burnett's 1978 landmark of Black independent cinema — a loose, lyrical portrait of a slaughterhouse worker in 1970s Watts — gets a rare 4K theatrical screening as part of the Film Society Center's LA Rebellion series. One of the foundational texts of American independent film, and it essentially never plays theatrically; a genuine chance to see it as intended, not on a laptop.

A hands-on, no-experience-required soldering class at Iffy Books: you leave with a working rechargeable battery pack for a microcontroller project (ESP32, Pi Pico, LoRa node), not just notes. $3.99 for the kit plus your own battery — about as low-stakes as DIY electronics gets, and exactly the kind of practical-skills programming that makes Iffy Books more than just a bookstore.

A free, no-cover queer social mixer built specifically for trans, non-binary, and gender non-conforming Philadelphians, running Thursdays at Tattooed Mom. 'We won't be erased. We've always been here' — community space as its own quiet political statement, not a themed party.

top3.why: DC215's monthly Third-Friday lockpicking night returns to Wooden Shoe Books — bring your own picks or borrow a set, no experience needed, novices and seasoned safecrackers side by side. The kind of hands-on, no-gatekeeping skill-share that fits Wooden Shoe's whole ethos: knowledge as something you're handed, not sold.

Philly's own purveyors of hot jazz and vaudeville revive the Black Squirrel Club's speakeasy bones with a set of Roaring Twenties and pre-war swing. Come early — doors are pushed up to 5:30 for a World Cup match on the back-room TV — and stay for a band that treats the genre as a living thing, not a museum piece. $18.50 advance, $20 at the door.

Free closing celebration for the Association of African American Museums' national conference, marking 50 years since AAMP became the first museum built and funded by a major U.S. city specifically to preserve Black history. Expect a performance from the Marian Anderson Choir and an interactive AAMP Disruption showcase — a genuinely rare night where the museum itself is the event, not just the backdrop.

top3.why: A five-band, all-ages benefit show at the Ukie Club — the Ukrainian American Citizens' Association's basement DIY room in Northern Liberties — with every dollar going to Savage Sisters, the Kensington harm-reduction org. Godcaster headline; Fib, Null, Taurus Judge, and Sodaseas round out the bill. Punk as mutual aid, not just a genre.

Iffy Books tables at Highmark Mann's free, campus-wide 50th-anniversary community day — build a solar-powered synthesizer, learn open-source DJ software Mixxx, browse zines by donation — folded into a day of hands-on programming tracing pivotal moments in Philadelphia history. Free, family-friendly, and a rare chance to get DIY-electronics programming somewhere other than a bookstore basement.

The 4th annual Philadelphia Bookstore Crawl — nearly 60 independent shops across the city, one day only — closes out at Head & The Hand with a 7pm panel of four debut authors: Samantha Paige Rosen, Yu-Mei Balasingamchow, Kat Stoddard, and Kim Narby. Hit any of the day's stops for stickers, discounts, and giveaways, but this is the one with a fixed time and an actual conversation.

top3.why: Luis Marrero's touring poetry open mic returns to the Loft at City Winery — a raffle-style open mic, a spotlight performance, a featured poet, a live DJ, and a painter working in real time, all built around storytelling and community rather than the venue's usual wine-list programming. A rare case of City Winery hosting something that isn't a legacy-act nostalgia tour.

Faetooth call it 'fairy-doom metal' — doom and sludge slowed down further, shot through with shoegaze haze and post-metal weight, built around folklore and the uncanny. They've been racking up real momentum (a KEXP session, a new headlining tour) without losing the DIY grime. All ages, $22-25.

The Columbus lo-fi legends who helped define the mid-2000s 'shitgaze' scene — blown-out, tape-hiss noise pop that somehow still hits like a pop song — are back on the road. A genuine reunion-era rarity for anyone who spent 2008 with 'Rip It Off' on repeat, at one of the city's best mid-size rooms.
